blocks.x: You might give your name again the way you usually start out our official interviews.
Yes. That's Harold Dejong.
And I'll mention...
Born on February 4th, 1999.
Yeah, I mentioned that they were doing this over at Ralph Collins' shop, 934 Bourbon, and the date is November 18th, and this is the second interview with Mr. Dejong.
Okay, what is your birth date again? 4th of February, 1909.
Where were you born? Just what part of town?
I was born on Conay between St. Louis and Conay. But I was raised around Tremay, you know, around St. Ann and Miro.
And your folks lived there long. Can you tell a little bit about your father? Was he a musician?

No, my father was not a musician. My father had it kind of tough coming up, but after he got to be drawn, he went on. My father told me, he used to tell me stories sometimes, he used to pound brick and sell brick to take care of his mother. Yeah, but after he came up, he started off with one mule and wagon. And he got to be the biggest colored boss dramman in his town.
What did he do with the- He was a dramman, he was a dramman.
Just like Maloney and Dyes and these other drammen.
Speaking of the brick business, I wondered, had he worked making bricks or what? No, he didn't.
No, no, no.
I've heard that some people would grind up the thing and use it as a cleaning powder. Well that's what they did. He did that.

And then days, I mean, because even when I was small, they used to do it also. You'd get these red bricks. Yeah, the real soft bricks. You see, soft brick. And it pounded good, see. And you'd get a little bucket, they used to sell a nickel bucket. And people used to, well you see, they didn't have nanoliums in the kitchen, so they'd scrub the kitchen floor with grandma and pot and lye and brick. And all that used to be beautiful, you know, and clean. And then people used to scrub the alleyway and sprinkle brick all in the alleyway. Yeah. When I was small, my mother used to make me scrub the steps outside, you know, I used to brick many days, at the pine, pine the brick and then, you know, scrub the steps. Yeah, that's what they used to use, scrubbing. I remember one time, I said, scrub three or four steps in a block, the people used to think I scrub them so good. My mother wouldn't let me take that. You know, they would give me two bits a piece, and that was big money in them days, a dime a piece. She wouldn't let me take.
I'm still wondering about that brick and dust, did it dissolve in water, or is it just like a little sand? No, no, no, they didn't put it in the water.

They didn't put it, they put it, see, like you're fixing to scrub, they'll sprinkle it on the floor. Now some people should mix it with the soap powder. Yeah. She'd mix it up with the soap powder. It's like a grit then.
That's right.

And then they'd take the scrub and brush and scrub, I guess it'd help to clean, it's like a grit. And then, like I tell you, some people are living in a corner house, where people always hang on the steps on the corner house, they didn't have barms to hang, you know, too many barms, or the youngsters couldn't go in the bar, but they'd all be on that corner house, they'd have the light on the corner, you see. Everybody would be sitting there, well some of the people didn't want you to sit on their steps, so when they scrub the steps, they'd sprinkle brick, set that brick on, see, so if you'd sit on your door and you'd close. Yeah.
I never saw that.

Yeah, well they used to do that a long time ago then, I mean, times changed, people were getting annoyance of putting in the kitchen and so forth and so on, I mean, well, they didn't use that no more. But man, you'd walk in any house, I would say, in a tram area, maybe in the seventh ward or ninth ward, you'd walk in them alleyways, you'd have beautiful brick, you know, and one had the reddest brick, the nicest brick, well the alleyway looked nice. And I think one reason for that sprinkling brick in the alleyway, I don't know if I'm right, but I do know, you walk in some people's alley that didn't have the brick sprinkled in it, from the dampness the bricks would be slimy, like you'd slip on it, you know. I think that's one of the main reasons. Yeah, that's right. So much of the moisture. Yeah.
You said brick dust to scrub floors, wood and two? Oh yeah, yes indeed.

Scrub the steps outside and see like people paint the steps now, a long time ago, even if the, wherever you rent your house from, the landlord, if he'd paint the steps, people would scrub the steps until they get that natural wood color in. Yeah. Put lye and this grandma powder, you know, a store powder called grandma powder and brick, scrub them steps, get all that paint off, let them steps look beautiful. Yeah. You're very, well I mean you didn't see many doing the steps, you can go sit on the steps with a white suit on.
No.

You know, the neighborhoods I was living in, because I always lived in a mixed neighborhood all my life. I mean, I didn't know nothing, I didn't, you know, never realized all this food was coming on was coming on now. Yeah.
These people are like crazy.
Yeah, you see the papers, let's go with that.
Well I, well I, well I mean I was up there driving through it, you know, yeah.

Well I mean I run from the 77th chapter 2 street to the Conway's building, and there was big parades of them was passing Brown Street. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, a couple of them kicked at the station wagon and kicked at other people's cars. I mean they have nothing, because the thing is this is even just kicking at the white people cars and everything. Yeah. They're fighting one another.
Yeah, just hoodlums.

Well you hoodlums, I think it, well what I think it is, uncontrolled teenagers that, you know, the people don't have control over them because I mean nobody would sense them doing nothing like that. Yeah, absolutely.
Can you tell us any more about when you were young, aside from music, anything that you

did to me? Yeah, well I mean I'm not, well I mean money wasn't plentiful like it is now, but you could do more with a dollar. In other words, I remember when I was small, well my little brother, he used to start after we had our little band got together, and my brother studied hard, he went right on, P-ron, you know, and when I was with, played with Riddler and these different bands, P-ron, before he went to P-ron they had a very good young band, about the best young band they ever had, and I don't think they'll ever have another one called the Sonny South. It was here, I think Sidney Montague was playing drums and I get there.
Is that one they had the picture of, the little picture?
No that's the Moonlight Syreners one. Oh sure.
That's our first band.
I'm talking about the first big band he played with.
Your brother was that? Yes.

How old was your brother? Well he should be 49. 49. Yeah. And well he, they had a very good band and then from that, then P-ron changed his band around where he went with P-ron. And well he used to come home at night and just like he'd make his money, put it on the dresser, and even I come in when I put half of mine. Well I mean my mother never, you know, wants to do it but he just did it. Was there anybody else in your family that played your mother?
Did she play anything? No, my mother didn't play, but my mother could sing well.

She didn't, you know, she was a professional then but she'd sing. She used to go to the opera all the time and you know sometimes she'd be, whenever she'd wash clothes, she'd be washing clothes or maybe in the kitchen and she'd have wonderful voice, you know, the opera voice.
New the opera or something, sing some of that something.
Yeah, she'd sing Carmen and all numbers like that. Yeah. Well see my grandmother, she couldn't speak English. She spoke French, you know. Very few things she could say.
Well I was going to ask you about, when did they speak in your home? Most of the French?

Well in my home my mother and father, we see in them days they didn't want the children to talk to them. I see like nowadays you go to people's house and they say anything in front of the children, you know. But in them days, well they'd speak, my mother and father would speak French, you see. And in fact that's how I learned a little bit how to speak, you know. There was some time my mother would, like on Sunday she used to send my grandmother her dinner, you know. And she'd tell me in French what to tell her and then when I'd go there my grandmother would tell me what to tell her bag, he'd say yeah. But I don't remember anyone else in my family playing music. I mean I wanted, my brother wanted the violin and I wanted the clarinet. And so my daddy bought him a violin, bought me a clarinet and we started taking that. How old were you when you started? I remember I was around nine, ten years old.
Which school did you go to?
Well I went to, I started at right here at St. Mary's, the Holy Family.
You were Catholic in the course?

Yeah Catholic on Arlene Street at the Holy Family. And then later on I went to Byer Road School. It's on Byer Road in Durban. I think it's Clark now isn't it? No it's not, Clark is on demand. I went to Byer Road and then moved to St. Philip Street. Oh yeah. Yeah well that's Craig, it's Craig School now. Byer Road. It was just a big house and across the street where you see all them raised houses, well that was a junior high there. Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Big house. But I had all good teachers and I think my second grade or my third grade teacher, she was a piano player and I used to go to her house sometime on Saturdays and run little marches down when she was going to play with a chair in the march after Stedford. Did they teach any music in the school?
Either band or orchestra or singing or anything? No they didn't. Well I mean like singing, yeah.
Well that was an everyday occurrence, you know, singing because you're singing maybe in the morning.
Did they teach the kids to read music in the school? Even when I went to school they didn't for a while.
Well they didn't, they did, if they did I don't remember. I think I should remember it.
Yeah, you should remember that.

No, because the first thing I ever, the first note music I ever took was with Professor Nickerson. And I never mentioned this to you, a Crump, a Frank Crump, when T.O. was away a while, before I went with Shalini a while, well he used to come at my house and give me music lessons, his name is Frank Crump. This fellow, I'm talking about Henry Julian, that's Henry Julian's brother-in-law. Remember I told you Henry Julian was a very fine clarinet, safe one place, his brother music back with George McCollum? Oh yeah. Well that's his brother-in-law. But he was, he was an old time around here and he used to come to help me out a while, you know, while T.O. was away.

I wanted to ask some more about the Nickerson and unfortunately I forgot, up at Tulane we had some old woods directories of all the colored businesses in town and they had a big ad, almost a half page ad I believe of the Nickerson School of Music and it seems to be one younger man, the one that specialized in violin and was it the old man, Professor Moneta, studied with the Nickerson, that would be the different one would it or the same one that you studied?
Well, I don't know of any other Nickerson.
I thought one was marked, was listed as Junior or something, do you know of that?

Well, no I don't know of that but I was very young and just like I tell Professor Nickerson was wearing moustaches and goatees and he was pretty much in age then. So, and if Moneta took less of one of them it might have been his father. Yeah, that's what I remember. It might have been his father.
Yeah, that might have been the Junior that would still look elderly.
Yeah, yeah, because I would say he was in his father's fifties when I was taken that sort of. He wore a goatee, you know, and moustache.
Well his father could have been...
He was pretty strict too.
His father could have been sixty or seventy.
Well sure he is, yeah. Two years ago, you know... See, because I met his daughter and his son, you know, his younger son.
The daughter is the one that's in Howard University now in Washington.
I'd like to see her someday, see if she remembers me. Yeah.

Yeah. I started to say, two years ago when Fess and I were out in California, we stayed at Johnny St. Cyr, and he had an old violin. It was in about twenty pieces. That's still over there. I never did put it together. But he said he picked it up in the garbage can and it had belonged to some Nickerson who played violin. And Fess says that was a nephew or something like that, or son of the one he took from that

thing. Well, yeah, well it couldn't be. The one that I was taking, that's what he had, was something called Dalton. I think it was Dalton. And he was, I think he's learned him music, but I don't guess that that viol would be, might be for Professor Nixon I know.
Might have been the man who studied with him.

I think so. I think that's what it would be. Because he had a lot of students, he turned some very good scholars out. Just like I said, my brother was a kid and he could play violin very good. And this boy Benny Harmon, with Leffier, he went to California and played with some white man, I don't know who or where, but I haven't seen him since. He was very, very good. In them days the boys was, they didn't carry knives and things like that, but they had little gangs and when they'd come take lessons at Professor Nickerson, they would make some of the boys take their instrument out and play for them. Right there in the grass, he said, I haven't learned anything yet, they'd say. Well play with your loins, learn the lessons, play the scale, anything. Well my brother and I would come along now, you can hear him say, it's Charlie's brother, don't mess with them.
Some of the tough kids up in the Irish channel used to do that too.

Well I was at the corner club, on 2nd and Russo, and it's like I tell you, I knew a lot of them fellas, in the commercial district, see, because on Saturdays I used to deliver bills for my daddy, you know, in places that he did business with I delivered him the bills. And a lot of them fellas knew my daddy from around the commercial district, but they never, so they never did make us do that. But they used to make the boys take, when they come from playing up in Irish town, take the instruments around, play us a tune man. Right there in the street, yeah, play a tune. Well if they go and act nice and play a tune, the instruments wouldn't get broke up or nothing, you know, so if they act nice and play a tune then they could go, you see.
Yeah, otherwise there were a tough bunch of them.

Yeah, it was a tough bunch of them. It was pretty much. The first job that, I think it was about the first job I never got paid on, I played at the corner club. I don't mean the club, the club paid them the job, but this fella by the name of Munson Hickman, he had a job and we was all youngsters, you know, and he got the money in front. See, and he went and take another job, he sent us on that job so we go to collect our money because we played the dance, the man said, well we paid Hickman off already. So we never get our money. Of course I never did tell my dad, because my dad wouldn't have found him, you know. Not that my dad needed the money, but just for the principal of the thing, yeah. That's about the first job, the fellas would call that a ham in them days, you know, like when you're in the job, you say, we took a ham tonight. When we was with Desdun, I think the first, when we left, we were going on that tour, I think our first night, I think it was sixteen or twenty-two dollars we made that first night. But we did good all the way going. And Desdun said, y'all wait till y'all hit my home. I bet we'll make forty or fifty dollars a man. That's the way he's talking to the horse. We get in his home, I think we made about twenty-five cents a man. Yeah. But we was not broke, we all had money. Because we did good all the way through. Yeah, we did good. But you see, his father, I could understand his father in that territory was just like Claiborne William was around here on the other side of the river. You see, around Donovan and that poison girl all along that. Very popular, anywhere they played, that crowd, you see. But they didn't take the son like they did the father.
Just where was his territory?
Desdun. Desdun, well around Omaha, Iowa, I mean around Nebraska, Iowa.
And we went up around Omaha.
Yeah, we went all the way to Omaha. We left here, we went to Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Iowa, and Kansas, and right on in Omaha.
His first name, was it Clarence? Clarence Desdun.
And how did he spell it?
You told me the other day, but I don't think we got it on him.
D-E-S-D-U-N-E. N. Yeah, D-E-S-D-N. Like in no, N. That's right. D-U-S-D-N-E.
Because I've seen the other side of the rhythm is another way.

He's a very good violinist, very good violin player. And I remember this well, he couldn't play that banjo too well, you know. He had one of the big, what do you call it, a plexon with that long neck on.
The five string one.

Yeah. And Harry would be playing some banjo. And sometimes he'd get in a break and a tiger, and Harry would feel like he had fun, he wouldn't make the break. He'd let it go, ploka ploka ploka, you know. Let that dude make it. Harry was a very good band to play with us.
Sorry we didn't bring that picture here tonight. Yeah. But do you remember who else was in the band? Well yeah.

I was going to tell you, Harry Faglitude on a banjo, Warren Bennett playing alto, Lucen Johnson was playing alto, I was playing tenor. And later on Warren Lesbavis got Oliver Alcorn, because Oliver made the tour with us. And because Warren, just like I told you, Warren wanted to go back to Mississippi and put that roof on his house. So when I had Warren was very good and Oliver was good and Lucien Johnson, well after Warren left the band, Lucien Johnson was playing the clarinet solos. And I was playing tenor and Felice Goff was with the band a while. Oral Fosier was with the band a while. Oral Fosier was on that picture. Because he started with the band you see. But I think he got a regular job or something. I don't know what caused him not to make the tour with the band. But he was with the band, the band was here. And Raymond Brown was playing trombone, that's H.S. Farnelow, very good trombone player. He and George McCullum was the only brass we had in the band. One trombone, one trumpet. But I'm telling you, it sounded like a full brass section. Because they really, you know, it was a powerful man to play. We had old man Kimbo playing tuba. And Kimbo was playing bass and banjo around there and he was a very good banjo player, Kimbo. Before he started playing bass, his dad was playing tuba with us. Very good tuba player. And we had a, I don't remember what piano player left here with us because, just like I say, Warren would play piano sometimes, because Warren was playing piano while Oyal Fosier was playing. So he's playing with the band you see.

By the way, one time there was a little brother Montgomery, he came from Mississippi. Did he ever bring him? We picked him up in Jackson, Mississippi. Well he played with us. He played with your son of Montgomery. He played with us at the same time. He made it too with us.

We picked, his name is Uro Montgomery. We called him little brother Montgomery. But we picked him up in Jackson, Mississippi. The same place we picked up Eugene Porter. You see, because some of the boys didn't want to make that long trip. We picked Eugene Porter up in Jackson, Mississippi and we picked brother Montgomery, little Uro Montgomery. Pick him up. And he could play some piano. He still does. He still works. He was down here last year. Yeah, well I'd like to see him. You know he got off the beam one time. Yeah, that's right. Yeah.
But he left us in Omaha. He had to go make some records.

He had to go, some blues singer, a woman he knew in Chicago had sent for him to make some records. He was in Omaha. But he could stop or dance. That's right. That boy would get in one of them cab rats and get to play on that piano. He had one blues he would play. People would actually stop dancing and come stand around that piano. That's right. They would stop in the middle of the floor and just get to walk and see them one at a time, something like a moving picture. You see them just walking by that piano. And he'd sing that blues and play that piano. And after he went we picked up a woman from Attacan, Kansas. Her name was Vivian. I don't remember my last name but man, could she play some piano?
Woo, woo.

Gee. We missed Brada for the blues that she could play, but we never missed them when she was playing in the band. She could play. She came all the way down here with us and played with the band a while and after things started to slow it up she went on back. But she was very good. In Kansas, huh? Yeah, she's from Attacan, Kansas.
Wasn't from the south originally?
No, Attacan, Kansas. That's her home.
Because we was booking a few jobs out of St. Joe.
We were playing like Kansas City. I thought we had that contest in Kansas City with Fender Harris' orchestra. And this, a baby, a drummer from here. He's a bright fellow. He looked like white.
One fellow I knew, I didn't think he was quite that light, but Baby Lovett, do you remember? Baby Lovett.
That's him. Yeah, he was very, to me.
He came from Alexandria. Well, I don't know what already dealt with him.

But he was playing with a band in Kansas City. And he told us, he said, listen, he and I, and Lucian Johnson, and a couple other boys in the band was together, and he said, don't y'all, we used to have all Ted Lewis arrangements, you know. He said, don't play nothing but the good old New Orleans jazz, which y'all really know how they play. They play high as a side, the Tiger Rags, the Sandler's Blues, you see, if y'all want to win this contest. And this band had some fine arrangements. I was enjoying that stuff, you know. And we playing all this old Stomp Down Dixieland, see, we had a good Dixieland outfit with us, you see. George McCullum, Ramon Brown on Trumbo, then Old Man Kimmel on Susan Fung, and after he left, no, in Kansas City, in Kansas City we had Baby Woods. Old Man Kimmel had then left the band then. We had a big fellow by the name of Baby Woods.
On bass.
Oh, yeah, a tuba. You ever know who Baby Woods? No, never knew.
He was a big, big fellow man.

And could he play that tuba? If a trumpet could take a solo and if Baby Woods had a few drinks and him not too high, just about right, he'd play that solo behind that trumpet on that sous-a-phone. I mean, North for North, beautiful. Oh man, he could play that sous-a-phone. Well we had him with us and he stood up and played a whole solo in Tiger Rang, making a terrific break in it and everything on the sous-a-phone. You know we won that contest. And I was wishing we had a band like that. Yeah. Well when we got there, I mean I'll tell you the truth though, we'd hit some town sometime and had bands like Sunset Royal, I mean wonderful bands. Yeah, I heard that. And they would come to our dance that night, they'd play, they'd close them up. People come here that band from y'all, you know. Sunset Royal had all them big fine arrangements, I mean all first class stuff. Well we'd play a band from y'all, they'd want to hear that Dixieland stuff. We'd play a little high to the side and shake it and break it and hang it on the wall, you know, stuff like that. You know what I mean? It really went. Yeah. Everybody went crazy about that music.
How did you travel in those days?
Well when I was with Risley we traveled in a truck. Just a truck?
Yeah, a truck man.

A truck with the tap oil on the side of it. Snow and ice and everything. Yeah, sitting in the truck like that, you overcoat it when you're traveling. And then remember Desmond, Desmond had a model A-Ford bus, a model A-Ford. Brand new model A-Ford they bought, and they first came out in 1930. No, around the last part in 1929 I think they came out. Yeah, around 29. Yeah, in 29. I'm almost sure. I wonder how they bought a brand new one. Had a red bus with a trans-design John A. Riddler on the side of it. And the model A-Ford left, yeah. We made a, I remember this very well because he talked about a tire we was using on the bus, I think it was a firestorm tire. We got a, we went 36,000 miles before we had a blowout on a flat tire. Yeah, well that was a little better than the truck you know, but still with the hard seats on the side you know. Was it heated at all? No, it wasn't heat man.
Nobody had heaters in the head. No, indeed though.

Heat though. It didn't know nothing about no heat. The time you heat from that motor you drive, you see we all used to take a 50 mile, we used to call it a 50 mile shift you see. I'd drive 50 miles, anybody that I'd drive would drive 50 miles, keep from getting too tired. Nothing but them old gravel roads most of them did. When you hit an asphalt road you was in heaven, you thought something was wrong. Yeah. We caught some terrible road, I remember around Nebraska. We caught some rain and that old red mud. And we had to stay in one town a couple of nights. That's right. The people liked the band so much, and that town, we were supposed to leave there the next day, we was going to make some kind of rain and get there the next town. He said look, the man said didn't know how bad the weather is, I'll call them along with this and I'll pay for it and tell them to get the truck fixed.
Play for us again tomorrow.

Yeah. I'm telling you, I never dreamed, you know you take what's happening now in the beautiful highway and stuff and taking them days and all the time and see how a place was traveling, you just can't hardly realize it you know. Now you're traveling with a nice bus, heated, you know, cooling system in it, or automobile with heat in it. Yeah, get a flat tire, you have a sweats light, something like that. I remember, I think in Punctitura, we were in front of the station, it was snowing and we was changing the tire in Ridgely's truck. Yeah, I remember that.
Can you tell us a little bit more about Ridgely's band, how they split up to East Salastan?

Well I don't know how he had to stand split up, I really don't know the story of it, but there was one, I think, I don't know if Mr. Porter was playing with Salastan, but when I went with Ridgely, Mr. Porter was playing bass with him and Mr. Porter was a kind of bass player, he must have come from some other good band.
He had a string bass, he played with the tuba mostly? Tuba, yeah.

He played, I never heard him. He had both instruments, I didn't know what you did. Yeah but I didn't know how he played string bass until later years, you know, he played tuba with us. Yeah, he had a, I can't remember this trombone player's name that was playing trombone with Ridgely, but it's some outstanding things that you never forget, you know. I remember we'd get in a room when we'd travel and all put traveling clothes on and this little trombone player, he stared in his tuxedo suit all the time. I mean he'd get on the band and say that night he'd look just as fresh as everybody else. Yeah, I don't know how he did that.
Well you told us about Ridgely played drums you said.
Yeah he played drums, yeah he was playing drums.
Was Keith going bad or why did he stop trombone, do you know?

Well no I don't know why he stopped trombone but when he was playing drums I think Gilbert Young was the one who got me with the band. Gilbert Young and Emma Barrett the bell girl, she was playing piano and Feliks Goff was playing tenor saxophone because sometime Mr. Porter, Feliks would take a solo on a clap and Mr. Porter grab his tenor saxophone and he'd be playing and let it blow by and you know one of them kind of things. He could play at saxophone too you know Mr. Porter. Yeah. And we'd travel around Mississippi and parts of Louisiana with Ridgely, but Ridgely used to get some of the choice jobs around him. Yeah. And after he went out, I went with Desdun, well Desdun had some good connection too. I guess Piro gave him a lot of jobs because he was a good violin player also. But there was some tough times but I'll be frank, which I enjoyed him. I really enjoyed every bit of it. Every note I played on the horn. You know I seen one time, we stayed about seven, eight days without even seeing a band. Just as happy as could be. Oh man.
I was going to ask one more question about Ridgely, did they both call it the Tuxedo Band? Is there any trouble about that? Yeah.

No I never heard no confusion about it. I never heard no confusion about it because I don't think Susie had copyright on it but when Ridgely made his band he called it Ridgely's Tuxedo Band. Yeah. And Celestad Celestad's Tuxedo Band. That's right, that's the name he went on, that's the way he played. Country club or Southern Yacht Club, everywhere. Ridgely's Tuxedo Band. And people liked him very much.
Can you tell us about Burnell San Diego?

Yeah, when Burnell was small I remember taking a clap and then sometime I used to pass at a place on North Claremont and Santa Ann and used to put Burnell stand on two Coca-Cola box by the piano to play. At that time they used to call it Bucking one of them, you know, Lil' Willie used to go there, Baby Bruce, Baby Bruce have a mechanic shop out there and Seminard project right now.
He's all good. Someday we'll go there.
He got a piano in his garage, he'll play a piano right in his garage.
That's good, don't forget that.

Baby Bruce they call him. Yeah, I'll make a note here too. Well Lil' Willie was one of them good piano players around there too. You see, just like I tell you, in them days, a boy like Lil' Willie, Baby Bruce, and they had nothing called Pruxum. I don't know his right name, but you know there's all good piano players around there, but Walter Pichon was class, more class. He could play the stuff they played and he was a musician on the boot of it. But he used to stand, boy, now on two Coca-Cola box then he'd be into the tandem much piano they play, he'd play it too. He'd stand up.
That's right.
He was that small, he'd have to stand on two Coca-Cola box to get to play the piano. That's right. I see like they made this boy, what's it called, Honey Boy, what's it called this kid?
Oh yeah, Honey Child.
